children: By Jiahui Huang and Fabiana Negrin Ochoa
Hong Kong has set ambitious goals to develop strategic industries and strengthen its role as a financial hub, including a plan to nearly double spending on technology and innovation.

The government's inaugural five-year plan targets increasing total domestic expenditure on "innovation activities" by around 10% a year through 2030, bringing the ratio of spending to gross domestic product to 3% after 2030.
That would be up from 1.63% in 2024, when spending on innovation activities--an umbrella term for research and development--totaled about $6.59 billion.

Like many other economies, Hong Kong has made sectors such as artificial intelligence a policy priority as technological advances play an increasingly important role in driving economic growth and remaining competitive.

In the five-year blueprint released Wednesday, Hong Kong also outlined plans to ramp up funding for manufacturing and so-called new industrialization sectors, which run the gamut from drug making to chip design and AI models. It set a spending target of 5.5% relative to GDP for manufacturing and industrialization in emerging industries, up from 3.8% in 2024.
The city didn't announce an economic growth target for 2030, but said annual GDP goals would be set in light of prevailing conditions.

The plan's focal points reflect the drivers of Hong Kong's recent economic rebound after years of subdued growth. A trade boost from AI-related demand and the stock market's resurgence have been key in reviving consumption and investment, helping the economy turn a corner.
Real GDP expanded at the fastest pace in nearly five years during the first half, prompting officials to lift their annual growth forecast to 3.5% to 4.5%.
Other goals underlined in the plan included boosting the tourism industry's value-add by up to 50% by 2030, banking on increasing tourism spending, which has underpinned the retail sector recovery.
Several other aims centered on making Hong Kong more competitive as a financial hub.
"Finance is Hong Kong's pivotal and crowning strength," the government said.

The city has been striving to heighten its appeal as an Asia base for corporations and asset managers, proposing tax reforms for fund managers and family offices, and concessions for gold and commodities trading.

Market authorities have progressively streamlined the process for public offerings, drawing a flurry of companies to tap Hong Kong's capital markets. Despite regulatory headwinds around dual listings, the city is one of the world's top initial public offering venues.
In an address, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee said authorities will look at further streamlining IPO requirements, including fast-tracking specialist tech companies' path to market.
Marcos Chan, head of research at CBRE Hong Kong, said that as the city's economy moves away from being services-driven, its future depends on the ability to seize opportunities in tech.

"The KPIs established in today's 5-year plan provide the market with a clear economic roadmap," said Chan, expecting that to give businesses a better gauge of potential demand growth and instill confidence.
